A Tang battle standard lies torn and ragged, half‑devoured by war. Across the faded cloth, brown streaks of dried blood spell out the soldiers' final vow.
The setting sun burns red, staining the shattered walls of the Howling Sand Outpost and sounding the last silent beat of the war drum.
A young soldier tastes blood rising in his throat, unable to speak another word.
Yet he holds fast to his oath. Like the desert poplar, he will stand unbending for a hundred years.

6830624377627560271:
Afflicted for so long, my destiny is spent. No salvation will come from heaven. All I have left are three unanswered questions that haunt me.

First, I ask of my uncle. You taught him the arts of war, he who mastered the ancient sutras of battle and saw into the very marrow of strategy. In his prime, he read the waning fire of the baleful star and knew the age of the Tubo was over. With a heart of iron, he vowed to return his homeland to the Tang.
But in the eighth year of Xiantong, my own father fell. You were bound for the imperial court, destined to die far from home. A seer told me your fate:
"He was blessed with opportunity, but cursed without the fortune, doomed to a premature and lamented death."
...Knowing such a cruel destiny, would you still have surrendered to it?

Second, I ask of my Emperor. We hold the Tang Empire as our heart. But if the Tang is our heart, why can it not see into our very core, into the loyalty that burns in our blood?
As I die today, my sole regret is a nation still at war. I lament that fate conspires against me, that our bonds are broken, that blades now point at me. But why... why does the knife that kills me come from within our own house?

Third, I ask of myself. This day, I am torn apart by the Uhu, betrayed by lesser men, and cast aside by the Tang. I search my entire life, and I ask... what great crime did I commit to be brought to this?

#N(The writing stops here, unfinished.)#E

Canghua was picked up by a Daoist from Jianlong Temple. 
The priests are vegetarian. Cats, obviously, are not. So Canghua often sneaks down the mountain, because the vinegar fish from Willowshade Village is divine. 
Canghua doesn't get it—with so many delicious things in the world, why do humans insist on making life harder for themselves? 
To seek the Way, you must starve? To become immortal, you must have no desires? 
Humans are strange. Canghua thinks, for the first time, that being a cat really isn't so bad. 
Humans seek the Way, cats do not. Humans crave ascension, cats will pass.

Yaoyao is the youngest of five siblings. 
She is utterly spoiled by the four older ones. That's why she's always smiling, bright-eyed and full of joy. 
One day, she passed the graveyard and heard a human voice. High and stirring one moment, low and tender the next. She didn't know what it meant, only that it was full of... something she couldn't understand. 
Her sister once said: humans love to sing. Was this their singing? 
She wasn't sure, but she wanted to understand. Why did humans sing every day, without ever getting tired? 
Since then, Yaoyao sits by the graveyard daily,
watching the humans "sing" as they come and go, again and again.
